rv.q: There’s Ruby, her daughter: thirtysomething, gorgeous and sensuous, who knows her worth, knows how to use it, and who is desperate to make something of herself. There’s Diamond, the stranger who walks into the club: a man worn sharp and hard through pressure, he claims to be Pearl’s estranged son and wants what he feels is owed to him.
But it may not have been a great idea for her debut play Driftwood to try and tell all of them at once.

There are contested memories with gentle shocks and apologies. It is beautifully done through their exchanges on the beach. Writer Tim Foley has won several awards for past works (including the Bruntwood prize) and it is clear, from the love and lyricism in this script, that he is a striking talent.

Unfortunately, this task proves too great a leap for White, whose grand emotive moments fall flatter than the others. Most of this is papered over by a masterful combination of technical factors, with lighting (Simon Spencer), set (Sadeysa Greenaway-Bailey) and sound (Tony Gayle) exchanging flashy moments, all of which come off with aplomb.
This riveting tale is a promising start for Laird as a playwright.
Still, anyone who believes in the idea that 'you reap what you sow' will find that principle works overtime in this somewhat intriguing snapshot of family and community dynamics.
However, the sheer volume of ideas competing for attention ultimately dilutes the play’s impact, making it harder for an audience to fully invest in its world and its characters.
Audibert has assembled a terrific cast in a highly wrought production

cn.t: Laird's ambitious debut set in 1956 Trinidad offers beautiful texture and an intriguing setting, but critics find it uneven, with too many storylines competing for attention in this family drama about colonialism and escape.
